note: This mutates the built-in `dict` ensemble at load time by reading its current -map, adding a new subcommand, and writing the map back; `dict getnull ...` calls later in the corpus resolve to a proc that is not textually 'dict' anything and is only reachable by reconstructing the runtime ensemble map (dicttool.tcl does this 5 times for getnull/print/is_dict/rmerge/isnull, each independently guarded by an info-commands check).

The ensemble's subcommand map is built by introspecting `info procs` at call time (not from any static list), then frozen into a *double-quoted* namespace eval string so $ensemble_map_of_type/$typeCommand are substituted before the inner script runs; later, huddle::unknown_subcommand (line 132) patches -map in place at runtime to graft in a superclass's implementation, so the set of valid subcommands for a given huddle type grows dynamically after first use and is impossible to compute without simulating both addType and every unknown-subcommand call.

Called ~10 times at file scope with a bare scheme name like `uri::register ftp { variable schemepart ... }` (line 1286); because register itself is a proc of ::uri, `namespace eval $scheme $script` implicitly creates ::uri::ftp, ::uri::file, ::uri::http, etc., and scheme bodies cross-reference each other via `[namespace parent [namespace current]]::basic::escape` -- so the full set of namespaces/variables that exist only comes into being by executing all the register calls, not by reading any single one.

Multiple complete implementations of the same API (e.g. ::json::parse_c vs a pure-Tcl one) live under suffixed names, and `rename` swaps which body is bound to the canonical name ::json::parse at runtime; a static resolver that treats 'proc json::parse' as a single fixed definition will pick whichever textual definition happens to load last, when in fact the live binding flips based on runtime accel-availability checks not visible at any call site.

Temporarily shadows the `set` builtin globally for the duration of this proc so that calling arbitrary generated API procs (which internally call `set` to declare config vars) is hijacked into recording data instead of assigning variables; any static resolver that hard-codes `set` semantics will misinterpret every `set` call anywhere in the process during this window, and the shim itself calls the renamed-away original via `::_set`.

Implements a chainable per-namespace unknown-command hook (using the real `namespace unknown`, not global ::unknown) where each `hook add` call (line 91: `Set $namespace [namespace code [list Handle $cmdprefix [Get $namespace]]]`) wraps the previous handler into a nested closure captured via namespace code; a handler signals 'fall through' with a non-standard `return -code continue -level 2`, so the actual command that runs for an unresolved name in some namespace can only be found by unwinding an arbitrarily deep, dynamically built chain of anonymous namespace-code closures.

Redefines ::unknown inside a throwaway safe child interpreter to a silent no-op so that evaluating an untrusted extracted 'catalogue' script never triggers Tcl's normal auto-load/'invalid command name' fallback; only three commands (pkgProvide/pkgIndex/fileoptions) are exposed back in via `interp alias`, resolved lazily at alias-creation time through `namespace which` in the caller's current namespace -- everything else silently vanishes instead of erroring, which a resolver assuming standard ::unknown behavior would misreport as undefined-command errors.

`nntp::nntp` creates an object-style command `::conn1` etc. via `interp alias`, but every subcommand it accepts (`_group`, `_connect`, ...) is dispatched by string-concatenating `::nntp::_$cmd` and checking `info commands` -- none of these are called by any lexically visible name anywhere in the file, only through this runtime-constructed prefix, so a caller of `conn1 group ...` requires resolving through both the alias and the computed dispatch to reach ::nntp::_group.

Available as a TclOO method-body helper (`link foo`), it creates an interp alias in the *object's own namespace* pointing bareword `foo` at `<objns>::my foo`; since `${ns}::my` is itself a TclOO-internal proc synthesized per-object at instantiation time (not a literal proc anywhere), and `ns` is resolved from the caller's frame at link-time, statically finding what `foo` invokes requires knowing which object instance is executing and its per-instance `my` dispatcher.

A safe child interpreter loads a plugin-supplied renderer file ($format, an arbitrary path) via the hidden `source` command, and the master then calls plugin-defined commands like `fmt_numpasses` inside it that exist nowhere in this source tree; simultaneously the child gets aliases like `file` and `dt_source` that silently jump back across the interp boundary into ::doctools:: procs in the master, so command resolution genuinely differs depending on which interpreter (master vs $mpip) a given bareword is evaluated in.

The trace callback is an anonymous `apply` lambda whose entire body is a string built at runtime (interpolating caller-supplied variable snapshots and the deferred script), registered on the unset of a shared sentinel variable to fire when the caller's stack frame is torn down; to cancel a specific deferred block later, the code re-derives which trace entry to remove not by identity but by `string match`-ing a comment marker embedded in the generated lambda body text against `trace info variable` output.

Registers a delete-trace on the currently running coroutine whose callback is an apply lambda capturing both the cleanup script and the caller's namespace (fetched dynamically via uplevel); the callback's home namespace is therefore neither the definition site of `finally` nor a namespace literal anywhere in the file, but whatever `namespace current` happened to be one stack frame up at the moment `finally` was called inside a `define`-generated generator body.

`Validate(integer)` etc. are ordinary global procs whose *names* happen to contain parentheses; `Validate($ProcDef(...))` in command position is not an array reference at all (no leading $) but string-built command-name construction -- Tcl substitutes the inner $ProcDef(...) value into the literal text 'Validate(' + value + ')' before parsing it as a command name -- so a resolver that pattern-matches `name(index)` as array syntax will completely miss that this is a dynamic call to one of ~20 procs defined 900 lines earlier.

The dispatch-table key `$linedata(action)` is parsed straight out of the raw text of an incoming IRC protocol line (attacker/server-controlled), and the value evaluated by `eval` is whatever command string a user previously registered via `cmd-registerevent`; there is no fixed, enumerable set of call targets here at all -- the entire dispatch table is populated and consulted at runtime inside a per-connection namespace created dynamically as `irc$conn::$host`.

A custom `oo::define` keyword (`Ensemble foo::bar {...} {...}`) never creates a method literally named `bar`; it splits the raw name, title-cases the ensemble part, and synthesizes `realmethod` = e.g. 'Foo_bar' via string concatenation, then defines *that* on the class while separately stashing a tailcall-dispatch stub string in a per-class clay dict (`method_ensemble`) that a runtime-generated switch body (built elsewhere in the file from that same dict) uses to route `foo bar ...` calls -- the actual method name backing any given Ensemble-declared subcommand exists nowhere as source text.

Adds a `classmethod` keyword to oo::define by, for every class created anywhere, silently also creating a shadow `<ClassName>.Delegate` class and mixing it into the class object itself (`self mixin`) so class-level method calls forward through it; `classmethod` then installs the real method on the *Delegate* of the class two frames up (`[info level -1]`) and wires the public name via `forward`, meaning the method actually invoked when you call `Table find ...` lives on `::Table.Delegate`, an object created as a side effect of every single `oo::class create`, not on Table or its declared superclasses.

For every incoming HTTP request a fresh object `::httpd::object::$uuid` is created and then has its class mixins chosen at runtime from a dict returned by `my dispatch $query` (URL routing) merged with ad-hoc `MIXIN_*` keys, ultimately calling into clay's `mixin` method which does `::oo::objdefine [self] mixin {*}$args`; which content-handling methods actually run for a given request is therefore determined by a routing table evaluated per-request, not by any static class relationship visible near the object's creation.

`result` is never declared or assigned directly in getoptions; it is passed by the literal name "result" into `GetOptionDefaults $optlist result` (cmdline.tcl:308-309), which does `upvar 1 defaultArrayVar result` and populates `result(...)` entries in getoptions's own frame as a side effect -- a resolver analysing getoptions alone would see `result` read from and never definitively written, missing that its contents are established entirely inside a different proc one upvar-hop away.

Inside a snit::type constructor, `upvar 3` / `uplevel 3` reach past snit's own object-creation machinery (the constructor call itself, snit's internal creation wrapper, and the `::page::util::flow` convenience proc) to link/execute directly in the scope of the original external caller of `page::util::flow`; the '3' is correct only because of snit's specific call-stack shape, so a resolver has to know snit's internals to know which frame `flow`/`current`/`$script` actually bind to.

Which stack level a user-supplied validation expression executes at (1 vs 2) is chosen by which of two nearly-identical option families (-validatecommand vs -validatecommand2) the procedure's caller used to declare it, driven by a literal `1`/`2` embedded in an unrelated foreach's iteration list; ValidateCommand itself is arbitrary Tcl text supplied by whoever defined the TEPAM procedure, so both the code executed and the frame it runs against are two layers of indirection removed from the call site.

The parser turns raw HTML tag boundaries into an unbounded number of embedded invocations of a caller-supplied callback name ($cmd, default ::htmlparse::debugCallback) directly inside the document text via regsub/string map, then `eval`s the entire synthesized blob as one Tcl script; the actual call sites for $cmd are not enumerable statically at all -- their count and arguments depend on the shape of whatever HTML document is parsed at runtime.

Every unqualified operator-looking call inside ::math::exact (e.g. bare `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` used later in the grammar actions) resolves through `namespace path ::tcl::mathop` rather than to any proc defined in this file; simultaneously the nested `::math::exact::function` namespace paths back to its parent, so a bareword like `sin` inside a `function::` body must be resolved by walking two independent namespace-path chains, neither of which is `namespace import`.

::tcl::mathop::* and ::tcl::mathop::+ are passed as first-class command-name values into the higher-order `foldl` (which later does `{*}$f $z $x`); a resolver must recognize the fully-qualified mathop command as a value flowing through a generic combinator rather than as an infix expr operator to know what actually executes inside foldl's loop.

Whether `package require try` lazily sources try.tcl or is a no-op, and whether `file::home` is provided as a builtin stub versus lazily loaded from fhome.tcl, both depend on the running interpreter's Tcl version at package-index-scan time; a resolver that just indexes pkgIndex.tcl ifneeded targets without evaluating the vsatisfies guards will get the wrong provider for a given Tcl version.

None of the exported commands (cov, fibonacci, max, mean, ...) are defined in this file; in a normal interpreter they only become resolvable by extending ::auto_path so Tcl's tclIndex-based auto_load machinery finds them in misc.tcl/combinatorics.tcl on first use, while in a *safe* interpreter (where autoloading is unreliable) the branch instead eagerly sources both files -- so the correct definition site for `math::mean` depends on a runtime `interp issafe` check, not on any import/require visible here.
